extracted.intended_audience: authors participating in PitMad or other Twitter pitch events (aspiring novelists seeking literary agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tips and evaluative guidance for composing, timing, and managing pitches for PitMad (Twitter) pitch events so authors maximize chances of an agent "like" and follow-up requests. Covers tweet content, scheduling, event rules, and next steps after the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of pitches / event hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Post within PitMad hours (the contest runs 8am to 8pm Eastern Standard Time) and choose times when agents are likely to browse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the east-coast concentration of agents and agency office hours (offices generally open at 10am). Recommended windows: 9–11am (burst of agent activity at the start of the day), lunchtime (people scroll while eating), and 4–6pm (day winding down). Stagger your three allotted pitches across the day rather than posting all at once early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey PitMad rules and agency querying guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow PitMad rules exactly and adhere to agency querying guidelines — agents test your willingness to follow rules as a proxy for how easy you are to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not break PitMad rules. Agents may post instructions about where and what to submit; follow those instructions when you receive a like. Also follow agency-specific query guidelines when submitting materials after a like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include images or GIFs (unless submitting a picture book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless you are pitching a picture book, do not attach a photo or use GIFs in your PitMad tweet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule prevents attachments for non-picture-book categories; adding images/gifs when not allowed violates PitMad guidelines and hurts your chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate hashtags (age category and genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include both an age category and a genre hashtag in your tweet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting to use both is against event expectations and reduces discoverability by agents searching those tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attention-grabbing typographical tactics (no ALL-CAPS) and don’t like others’ pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ALL-CAPS to stand out and do not like another author's pitch as a tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All-caps is explicitly forbidden as an attention device. Liking other authors' pitches to manipulate visibility or reciprocity is frowned upon and may be noticed by organizers/agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not game the system (no replying to get extra pitches or duplicate-tag cheating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not try to cheat for extra pitch opportunities by replying to 'Post your pitch here' tweets with the PitMad hashtag or otherwise manipulate tweet counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers and agents know such behavior and it harms your credibility. Also avoid creating duplicate tweets; Twitter hides duplicate tweets, so if you keep using the same pitch, reorder hashtags rather than repeating word-for-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing quality: concise, compelling pitch under 280 characters with proper grammar and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Your pitch must be both compelling and readable within Twitter's 280-character limit — do not sacrifice grammar and flow to cram in more words or text-speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shorthand and deliberate misspellings ('prper grmr', 'u', 'n2', etc.). Clarity and smooth flow matter: don't forgo proper grammar & flow so you can cram as many words as possible into your pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your three allotted pitches strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Rank-order your three pitches and post the best one first; if it fails to get a like, move to the next pitch rather than posting all three immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of sheer pitch volume, spacing and strategy matter. If one pitch gets a like, keep using that pitch but change the hashtag order to avoid Twitter marking it as a duplicate tweet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare submission materials in advance and follow agent instructions after a like
rubrics_metrics.description: Have your query letter, synopsis, and sample pages ready to send promptly when an agent likes your pitch and requests materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most agents will tweet instructions on where and what to submit the day of the event. Fast, correct follow-up increases your chances; consider getting query/sample pages critiqued ahead of time (author offers query critique services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PitMad as an agent-discovery tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Search Top Tweets under PitMad hashtags to find agents who liked pitches similar to yours and add them to your query list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top Tweets show pitches that received many agent likes — these signal multiple agents actively seeking that type of book. If you see a pitch similar to yours with agent likes, those agents may be good cold-query targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from the event and iterate if you don’t get likes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not getting a like doesn't mean your work is bad; use the event to study pitches, identify what works, revise, and continue agent hunting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read pitches as if you were an agent, analyze the ones that got likes, find critique partners, revise your pitch and materials, and try again in future PitMad events.
